Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors:  7-day history of daily fever with alternating chills/hot sweats, generalized myalgias, nausea with ↓ appetite, fatigue; recent adventurous travel through rural Vietnam 4 weeks ago with river/farmland exposure; no focal infective symptoms identified.  
- Relevant family medical history:  Father died of myocardial infarction at age 68.  
- Medications (including OTC or shared medications):  
  • Seroxat (paroxetine) – dose/route/frequency not documented  
  • Ibuprofen – OTC, dose/frequency not documented  
  • Paracetamol – OTC, dose/frequency not documented  
- Immunisation status reviewed:  Up-to-date for occupational (nursing) requirements, including Hepatitis B (per patient report).  
- Sexual and reproductive health:  Not recorded.  
- Physical activity and nutrition:  Moderate exercise a few times per week; current poor oral intake due to nausea.  
- Alcohol, tobacco, and substance use:  Non-smoker; moderate alcohol intake (quantity not specified); no other substance use recorded.  
- Hearing loss or concerns:  Denies ear pain or problems; no hearing concerns reported.  
- Mood/mental health (including depression, self-harm risk):  On paroxetine; no further mental health details elicited.  
- Vision problems or recent changes:  Not recorded (reports screen-related headaches but no visual change discussed).  
- Family and social relationships, caring responsibilities:  Works as a nurse; finding work difficult due to fatigue; no other social or caring roles recorded.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: 30-year-old woman with 1-week persistent febrile illness, night sweats, myalgias, nausea, and recent rural Vietnam travel. No localizing symptoms on ROS.  

Working diagnosis: Probable infectious etiology—malaria or other travel-related infection most urgent to exclude.  

Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript and DDx):  
• Malaria – high likelihood given endemic exposure and current symptom pattern.  
• Acute systemic viral illness (e.g., influenza/COVID-19) – moderate likelihood; common but less typical at 7 days without respiratory features.  
• Dengue/other arboviral infection – lower likelihood; exposure compatible though onset slightly late and no rash.  

Plan:  
1. Urgent in-person clinical examination at central London clinic (or local ED if unable).  
2. Blood tests: malaria thick & thin films, full blood count, inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR), basic chemistries; additional infectious screens as guided by exam (e.g., dengue serology).  
3. Advise patient not to attend work until evaluation completed.  
4. Administrative team to arrange same-day clinic appointment; patient provided contact number.  
5. Safety-net advice: attend A&E if symptoms worsen, rigors develop, or unable to access clinic today.  

Management Plan

- Immediate actions: Arrange same-day examination and blood tests (malaria films, inflammatory markers).  
- Medication advice: Continue paracetamol/ibuprofen for symptom relief within recommended doses.  
- Work certificate: Advise absence from work pending assessment.  
- Patient education: Discussed need to identify infection source; explained testing process and urgency.  
- Follow-up: Clinic review today; further management contingent on results.  

Consider:

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Physiotherapy already in place for chronic back pain; no new referral recorded.  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral:  Not recorded.  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded.  
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):

1. Malaria – High likelihood: Returned from endemic area; cyclic fever/sweats; rural exposure; prophylaxis not fully protective.  
2. Acute systemic viral infection (influenza/COVID-19/other) – Moderate likelihood: Non-specific febrile illness without focal signs; common community pathogens.  
3. Dengue or other arboviral infection – Low-Moderate likelihood: Endemic exposure plus fever and myalgias, but timing and absence of rash reduce probability.  

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note):
● Missing elements: Vital signs (BP, pulse, temperature); anthropometrics (height, weight, BMI, waist); detailed alcohol quantity; comprehensive mental health screening; sexual/reproductive history; urinalysis; vaccination record details; preventive screening status (Pap/HPV, STI, lipids, BGL).  
● No contradictions noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear but telephone format limited physical findings; some minor audio gaps but clinical content adequate.
